title: The better L2 gets, the farther it is from L4: the self-driving route war
dek: Pony.ai's Lou Tiancheng argues L2 and L4 have different goals: L2 users just need good enough and cheaper, so the better it gets the farther it is from L4; L4 needs ten thousand hours without an incident, and it needs a ruler for judging good from bad.
why: Lou Tiancheng lays out the time-scale ladder for self-driving, the evaluation system, and the competition-style strategy of holding your cards, and explains why end-to-end can only get you to 100 hours. High information density; the second half opens up into worldview.
who: Founders, investors and engineers working on autonomous driving, Robotaxi and L4 deployment; also for anyone who wants to see how Lou Tiancheng runs a company with a competitor's mind.
skip: If you only care about the technology and the business, the competition and personal-history section after 44 minutes can be skimmed.

points.h: Driverless is the real shock that breaks out of the circle
points.body: Wuhan's Apollo Go drew attention, and Lou Tiancheng says fleet size and a wider trial area are only that 1%; 99% is driverless. A person sitting in a car with nobody in the driver's seat, even with a safety driver beside them, is a completely different kind of shock; if this opening had been even 10,000 or 100,000 vehicles but with one person still sitting there safely, it absolutely would not have had today's effect. So why Wuhan caught fire may have something to do with the city, but that is definitely not the only reason. He is also trying to find out why Tesla pushed Robotaxi from August 8 to October, and says traditional L2 assisted driving is not driverless, and whether it can cross that 99% is a very different matter.

points.h: 100 to 1000 hours is stuck on the evaluation system
points.body: He describes self-driving in terms of 1 hour, 10 hours, 100 hours, 1000 hours, 10000 hours. 1 to 10 relies on the base model, 10 to 100 relies on data collection and complex models, and 100 to 1000 is most critically about evaluation: last month you did 200, this month the new version is 220 or 180, and you cannot guess, and you cannot just run for one hour; run for ten thousand hours and you are affected by rain, roadwork, heavy traffic on Friday night. You have to strip out all that noise to really judge whether you are doing well. His main energy goes into the contest based metric system, as it is called internally. This is a capability beyond resources, otherwise no matter how much money, data and machines you have, you are just spinning in place.

points.h: Different goals are what produce different routes
points.body: On the route war, Lou Tiancheng says only the goals differ. Where you want to go and where you finally arrive differ the most; the route only determines how fast and how close. He compares lidar to a cheating student who looks straight at the answers, and pure vision to a good student; the city thinks even an excellent good student struggles against a cheating student, so for full driverless you choose lidar. Tesla's pure vision is because it does not need to do full driverless, the passing bar is lower, and there is also cost and the delay on vehicle appearance. After a test drive, He Xiaopeng said Tesla FSD will definitely catch up with Waymo next year; he disagrees: L2 and L4 are not a like-for-like comparison, one is like football and one is like basketball, the evaluation standards differ, and the better FSD gets, the farther it is from L4.

points.h: The better L2 gets, the farther it is from L4
points.body: L2 users only require a big V1, so an L2 product can lower the metric from 10 to 8 because of cost reduction; that is a better L2, yet it is farther from L4. Because L4 needs 10,000 hours without an accident. He says incremental self-driving got a bargain: why do L2 first and then L4, rather than the reverse? L2 and L4 have different goals, and the essential technical difference means FSD definitely cannot achieve L4. Lidar is the cheating student, physically measuring distance directly with active light; L4 is an exam at the level of ten thousand questions, and the pure-vision good student may study for a long time while the lidar student looks straight at the answers. Beyond safety metrics, speed and comfort are also part of the evaluation.

points.h: After you surpass humans, data becomes a distractor
points.body: Before 1000, the more data the better; after you exceed the average human level, the more data the harder it is to converge. Because human driving behaviour in the data varies enormously, the model does not know whom to learn from, and it cannot take an average. He mentions Edo saying that when there is a lot of data the gradient quickly drops to 0 and cannot converge. He also gives his own example: he has reached 6000, and adding another 1000 of data pulls him back to 4000. Data is not to be thrown away but processed, so that only the useful part remains. End-to-end improves generalisation, and more data can help generalisation, but once you surpass the average level of the data, data becomes a distractor, and the more there is the harder it is to surpass.

points.h: Giving up on your original aspiration is not about hardship, it is unrealistic temptation
points.body: Eight years into the startup, Lou Tiancheng says the biggest temptation is that you could absolutely build something that commercialises in one or two years. Mr. Yao Qizhi spoke of not forgetting your original aspiration, and he later understood that the second half — holding fast to your original aspiration — is the truly hard part. Most people think giving up your original aspiration is because you hit many difficulties, but the real reason is unrealistic temptation; many people can hold on in the face of hardship, yet cannot hold on in the face of temptation. Many companies that came out back then, whose names are now unknown, did not persist, and it was basically not because of hardship or lack of money, but because they could not withstand temptation. So he treats self-driving as the ultimate direction for several generations of technical people, and is willing to wait another three to five years.

points.h: The competition master holds his cards: Hold hard
points.body: The competition technique Hold hard: there are things you know how to do, but you simply do not let people know, and by some means you make your opponent think you do not know either, so he gives up the idea of really going all out. For example, everyone is at 80 points and you can actually do 90; if you let the opponent know, he will dig out his potential; so you control your score, let him think you are about the same, boil the frog in warm water, and draw your sword at the last moment, when the opponent has no time to react. But running a company is different, it needs publicity, and intermediate results, making friends and partners all matter. Leading midway through a competition does not mean winning in the end, but a company cannot move the card-hiding play over.

points.h: AI surpassing humans is not AI's peak
points.body: Lou Tiancheng says a human is just an agent too, and asking whether AI will surpass humans is too high an opinion of yourself — what makes you think a human can judge whether AI can surpass humans. AI itself is a fitting-and-regression process, it has not created any new logical range, and today's large models are only mimicking human behaviour, far from artificial general intelligence. But he is not mystical, and he also admits this approach may be very good and may surpass humans. He also says the human energy efficiency ratio is terrifying: a meal and you are still not hungry now, and the same energy given to a robot would long since have failed; the heart beats this many times in a lifetime without breaking, and it cannot be built. He even thinks the world may be a simulator, and that the speed of light is an important parameter.
